keypoints.name: Controllability
keypoints.description: The ability to reach any state in a finite amount of time, and influence the system through actuators.
keypoints.strength_reasoning: Controllability is defined, explained with examples (monorail, car, beam), and revisited throughout the video.
representative_quotes: Controllability means that there exist control signals which allows the system to reach any state in a finite amount of time.
If it's uncontrollable, you have to address that problem by changing the system or the actuators.

keypoints.name: Observability
keypoints.description: The ability to know all states from the outputs of the system, using sensors and sensor locations.
keypoints.strength_reasoning: Observability is defined, explained with examples (car, monorail, beam), and its importance is stressed throughout the video.
representative_quotes: Observability means that all states can be known from the outputs of the system.
If any one critical state is unobservable, then the entire system is deemed to be unobservable.

keypoints.name: State Estimation
keypoints.description: Inferring the values of unmeasured states using available information (sensors).  A trade-off between sensor cost and estimator sensitivity.
keypoints.strength_reasoning: Covered in a dedicated section when discussing how to choose which states to measure directly.
representative_quotes: Being able to estimate a state using available information is good enough to claim that the system is observable.
Estimating states is a good way to reduce the hardware complexity of your system.
